articles.title: We Asked 45 People Over 80 About the Secret to Happiness—And They All Wished They’d Known This One Thing Earlier
articles.content:
Today I have answered 500(ish) emails, sent 300 texts, driven five teenagers to the mall, cleaned up four piles of dog vomit, taught three fitness classes, done two interviews, written one-and-a-half articles, attended one Spanish class … and it’s not even dinnertime yet. All that’s missing is the partridge in a pear tree. So my life is certainly full. But is it fulfilling? I can’t exactly say that all these things today brought me joy. But if we want to be Truly Happy aren’t we supposed to be, like, finding joy in the little things? Or something?
It’s that “or something” that I think about a lot these days, as the days fly by ever faster. Where are we supposed to find that happiness for our “one beautiful life” when it’s just so dang busy? Then it occurred to me that while we’ll ask 500 strangers online how to do sourdough bread, for some reason we never ask the people who’ve been doing this life thing for 80 years or more how to do life. Thankfully, I can fill that gap for all of us.
I write the 100 Years Strong column for The Healthy, where I interview people in their 80s, 90s and 100s about their lives and longevity secrets. I make it a point to ask each one what their secret to happiness is. And make no mistake: These people are happy happy. Even though they’ve lived through the Great Depression, World War II, the Civil Rights Movement, multiple revolutions in other countries and the full gamut of difficult personal challenges, nearly all of them are pretty positive most of the time.
“That doesn’t surprise me one bit. People do tend to get happier as they get older,” says Robert Waldinger, MD, a psychiatrist and the co-director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, the longest-running study of happiness in the world. If there’s one person who has interviewed more elderly folks than I have, it’s definitely him. “It’s a real, documented thing, called the positivity effect,” he explains. “There’s a psychological shift around the mid-40s, when people begin to realize life is short.”
To help find out what makes people happy, I interviewed more than 45 people, aged 80 to 103, and asked them what they wish they’d understood about happiness sooner and what keeps them smiling. Read on to find out. The answer will definitely surprise you—it’s basically the opposite of what the self-help section says.

The hard-earned secret that comes up most often among our folks can be best summed up by 100-year-old Dwight Roberts: “I don’t even think of life in terms of happiness. My mind doesn’t work on that level.”
Yep. The secret to happiness may actually be … not pursuing happiness. Or even thinking about it all that much. Most of the active 80-, 90- and 100-year-olds I talk to are so busy, staying useful and curious, that they never stop to grade their own happiness.
Connie Carr, who is still teaching three fitness classes per week at 93, agrees, saying, “Oh, I haven’t got time to be sad! I never have. With my hobbies and friends and classes, I’ve always got something happy happening.”
Havi Stander, 95, also keeps herself happily busy—including posing for a “not-so-nudie” YMCA calendar! “When people ask me about being happy, I tell them to stop focusing so much on yourself. Relax. Stay interested in everything around you. Don’t close your eyes, baby. There’s a wonderful world out there.”
Dr. Waldinger explains: “Happiness isn’t necessarily a choice—it’s a feeling. And the trick is to stop trying to ‘create happiness’ but rather create the conditions for happiness and then go on living your life.” He began exploring this theme in his first book, the New York Times bestseller The Good Life, and now offers practical tips for achieving this mindset in his new book, Nothing to Fix. Trying to force happiness can backfire. Just think of the parent gritting their teeth through a Disney meltdown, insisting, “This is fun, dang it, and you will enjoy it!” Instead, Dr. Waldinger suggests creating opportunities for happiness without demanding that every moment deliver *jazz hands* JOY.
Martha Clement, 91, who was delivered by a doctor in a horse and buggy and now uses AI, illustrates this principle perfectly. “I don’t get low because I get out and go,” she says, laughing at her rhyme. “Friends make me happy, but you can’t make friends or have friends if you stay home all the time and sit in that chair.” (Fun fact: The man who sat next to her in the interview, Lee Penhallegon, 90, has been her friend for more than 80 years.)
They’re not sitting at home making spreadsheets about how to optimize their happiness and cutting out every person who doesn’t “bring them joy.” In fact, these people are incredibly tolerant of things that make them uncomfortable or don’t go smoothly.
Dwight, for example, has run more than 300 races over the past 45 years, including four marathons, and still has the audacity to tell me he “still doesn’t like running.” So if the running doesn’t make him happy, why do it? Because running has given him more than the experience of running itself. There’s the thrill of a race, new friends, a sense of accomplishment and the benefits of staying active. As he puts it, he’s learned to skip the happiness audit and “just pay attention to what’s in front of you.”
Of course, my interviewees aren’t necessarily representative of everyone their age. They volunteered to talk with me, so it’s possible they were happier or more engaged than their peers on average. Still, the idea that we don’t have to feel happy all the time to live a satisfying life has support in psychological research. “Many many studies have shown us that optimism has a strong effect on health,” Dr. Waldinger says, explaining that not only do people who live longer feel happier, but happier people also tend to live longer, creating a beautiful cycle of positivity.
Boy does it! A 2024 UC Berkeley study found that monitoring and judging your own happiness was linked with lower well-being and more negative feelings—even during positive experiences. Simply wanting to be happy, however, wasn’t associated with those same problems. It’s a nuanced distinction. A 2024 Dutch survey of 8,331 adults found that people who valued happiness reported greater life satisfaction, but intensely focusing on being happy didn’t predict greater life satisfaction a year later.
This distinction matters: It’s fine to want to be happy. It’s the constant checking and nitpicking—Am I happy yet? Why aren’t I happier? What’s wrong with me?—that can get in the way.
Dr. Waldinger has seen this in his own research and personal life as well. “One of the things that I wish I knew about happiness sooner is that life is unsatisfactory. It’s not a flaw—it’s the point. I learned that studying to become a Zen priest,” he says. (Yes, he is a Zen master on top of being a researcher, psychiatrist, speaker, author and family man.) “It changed my outlook because I stopped trying to fight the discomfort and instead looked at what it is trying to teach me.”
It turns out that some of our unhappiness comes from trying so hard to avoid being unhappy—which, if we’re honest, is something many of us spend a lot of time doing. “One of the things I really focus on in my new book is the power of embracing our negative emotions, facing them head-on,” he explains. “Denying those feelings just makes it harder to act and to effect positive change. You can have unhappiness but still be happy.”
Dwight is the poster child (grandfather?) for this attitude: “Oh, I’ll have a great day today,” he tells me, even though it’s quite early and most of the day still stretches ahead of us. “Even when it’s a bad day, I always have a good day.”
Overall, strong relationships with other humans is the strongest link to both health and happiness, Dr. Waldinger says. But there are so many ways to build and maintain those relationships, which leads to three other main themes I noticed in my interviews.
Volunteer work, whether it’s through a formal organization or just helping out where you can, has been consistently linked to better health and increased happiness. Serving others is a powerful way of building happiness without focusing on it, because you’re absorbed in helping build someone else’s happiness, which, in turn, gives you more happiness than any self-care day could. And these seniors are living proof it works.
Edward Krauss, 91, ran his town’s food pantry for 23 years, built homes for Habitat for Humanity and then started his own charity building wheelchair ramps for people who can’t easily leave their homes. He’s still at it.
Jean Hinkle, 92, started a free lunch program and now hands out 100 to 350 hot meals every third Thursday. “God just put it on my heart,” she says.
Natalie Grabow, 80, the world’s oldest woman Ironman champion, is motivated, in part, by wanting to stay strong enough to care for her husband. “It gives me energy. It gives me joy.”
And Stephen Broadbelt, 91, who has lived all over the world and actually serenaded me during our interview, brings a dozen roses to church every week. He leaves a note inviting people to take one and give it to someone else along with a compliment. “At the end of the day, we’re all here to help each other,” he says.
But I think James Sneed, 103, sums it up the best. James drove a tank during World War II when the Army was segregated—he was actually pulled out of victory photographs and replaced with a White soldier—and went on to play a pivotal role in the Civil Rights Movement in the South while building several houses by hand and raising five children. Through it all, he maintained his faith in humanity and made a point of welcoming the people he met. “Do all the good you can, to all the people you can, every place you can,” he says. “That’s really it. That’s how you be happy.”
Friends of different ages and backgrounds can introduce us to new perspectives, experiences and opportunities to learn.
Ruthie Vinette, 96, spent her life on the water and made it her mission to bring swimming to underprivileged kids. When I asked about her friendships, she told me: “I [had] very good friends. And most of them are gone. So I have new friends, and all my friends now are younger. And I like that. They make me feel young, and I keep learning new things.”
Martha Clement and Lee Penhallegon, meanwhile, have been friends for more than 80 years. As they’ve grown older, they’ve continued to make new friends too. They begin by counting the classmates they’ve lost and remembering them fondly, then turn to the people they’ve met more recently.
“Making friends doesn’t have to be so complicated,” Lee says. “My rules are: Don’t gossip, stay easy to be around and keep showing up at the same places.”
Honestly, that’s a pretty good friendship manual at any age.
Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, many of us start treating fun as something we have to earn after all the important stuff is done. But if you want a life that feels good to live, recreation can’t always be the thing that gets bumped to next week.
Sonny Veltri, 98, decided to become a lifeguard in his 80s. Who starts a new hobby or side hustle at this age? Happy people, that’s who. When I ask him why, he gives me a sly wink and says, “For the ladies!” And not only does he thoroughly enjoy his pool time, but at 90, he also jumped in and rescued a drowning girl, providing CPR until EMS arrived, and saved her life. “You have to believe in yourself and stay positive when trying new things,” he says. “Don’t overdo anything. And always exercise—that’s the whole key. And keep laughing. I don’t know if that’s the secret, but it doesn’t hurt.”
Sue Foster, 91, who runs a large Airbnb agrees, saying, “I truly believe in humor as medicine. There’s nothing better than a good laugh.” So she looks for hobbies that give her that daily dose, like her classes at the YMCA.
Hobbies don’t have to be physical, though. Fred Richman, 99, a renowned artist who is selling more pieces than ever, tells me his motto is “Never act my age!” And then he admonishes me: “Please don’t tell me you’re going to act your age.”
Similarly, Mike Zambrano, 95, started dancing as a child in Cuba and kept that skill after he fled to the U.S. after the revolution. He danced everything from the bolero to the twist with his wife, and he still dances several times a week. “You can just make up your own steps if you can’t follow the rhythm,” he assures me. Which, frankly, sounds like excellent life advice beyond the dance floor.
The big lesson from my interviews is simple: Build a life that keeps you engaged with people and activities you care about. Give happiness room to happen instead of making it just one more thing to accomplish.
“Our brains are wired to look for danger, because negativity can be protective—it helps us spot threats,” Dr. Waldinger explains. “But that instinct can go into overdrive.” Between the 24-hour news cycle and the online “if it bleeds, it leads” mentality, we’re bombarded with danger signals, even when those threats have nothing to do with our own lives. “You have to consciously counteract that instinct.”
Here are six ways to start.
Instead of chasing a feeling, focus on the things that make life meaningful: spending time with people you love, doing something you’re curious about, helping someone else or simply enjoying what’s in front of you. Dwight Roberts puts it this way: “I ask myself, What can I still do, and what does it give me right now?”
That doesn’t mean pretending everything is wonderful. It just means changing the question from Why aren’t I happy? to What am I looking forward to? Who can I connect with? What would make today feel worthwhile?
If there’s one theme that comes up again and again among people who’ve lived long lives, it’s the importance of connection. But meaningful relationships don’t happen without effort. Sometimes you have to be the one who reaches out, makes the plan or shows up somewhere often enough that familiar faces become friends.
Put time with friends and family on your calendar instead of hoping you’ll find time later. Return to the same class, club, volunteer group or community gathering. And don’t limit yourself to the people you already know. Some of the most rewarding friendships can begin when you step outside your usual circle. It might feel awkward at first. Do it anyway. Friendship is worth a little awkwardness.
“We benefit from all types of relationships, and investing in relationships is the No. 1 thing you can do to be happier,” Dr. Waldinger says.
Helping someone else can give your day a sense of purpose that you can’t get from focusing exclusively on your own happiness. That doesn’t mean you need to volunteer for a major cause or become the person everyone calls in a crisis. It can be as simple as checking on a neighbor, sharing a skill, making someone laugh or finding a way to contribute to a community you care about.
All—yes, all—of the people I spoke with found meaning in service, volunteering and showing up for others. Their stories were a reminder that purpose doesn’t have to be grand or glamorous. Sometimes it’s simply knowing that someone else’s day was a little better because you were part of it.
Play isn’t just for kids! Whether it’s dancing, learning a skill, exploring a new place or doing something that makes you laugh until you can’t catch your breath, enjoyment deserves a place in your life—even when you have a thousand other things to do.
You can also make a habit of noticing the good things that are already there. One simple way to do this is to keep a daily gratitude journal. Another idea? Take a picture of things that make you happy when you see them, then put them into a digital scrapbook that you can keep adding to.
The goal isn’t to turn happiness into another assignment on your to-do list; it’s to give you more opportunities to find happiness organically.
“The nice thing about happiness is that even small changes can lead to an immediate happiness boost,” Dr. Waldinger says. Help someone today, even just give someone new a compliment, and see how you feel. However, to feel a change in your general baseline mood, it might take a bit longer. Expect a couple of months for the habits to feel automatic. After a year, you’ll see some real gains in well-being.
And don’t feel defeated if you fall off the bandwagon. It happens to the best of us! Accept the slip as a normal part of being human, not as a referendum on your own worth, Dr. Waldinger says. In fact, the UC Berkeley study found that judging your own happiness only adds negative feelings. So cut the “I should be feeling happy …” and replace it with “I’m feeling upset right now, and that’s normal and OK—here’s what I am going to do differently tomorrow.” You can and will recover from a bad day, a bad month or even a bad year.
Of course not! You’ll have days when you don’t feel happy, weeks when your plans fall apart and stretches when finding the energy to do much of anything feels harder than usual. That’s being human, not failing at happiness. The point isn’t to be cheerful all the time. It’s to keep making room for connection, curiosity and things that give your life meaning—even when you’re having a rough patch.
And it’s never too late to start something new. Just ask Natalie Grabow, our 80-year-old Ironman champion.
“I didn’t even learn to swim until I was 59 years old!” she tells me. “People think motivation fades with age. But if anything, it gets clearer.”
Maybe that’s the real secret: You don’t have to figure out how to be happy forever. In fact, there’s no such thing as happiness forever. Instead, keep living, keep connecting with others, stay aware of what does make you happy and stay open to whatever tomorrow brings.

And don’t limit yourself to the people you already know. Some of the most rewarding friendships can begin when you step outside your usual circle. It might feel awkward at first. Do it anyway. Friendship is worth a little awkwardness.

“We benefit from all types of relationships, and investing in relationships is the No. 1 thing you can do to be happier,” Dr. Waldinger says.

Find ways to be useful to other people

Helping someone else can give your day a sense of purpose that you can’t get from focusing exclusively on your own happiness. That doesn’t mean you need to volunteer for a major cause or become the person everyone calls in a crisis. It can be as simple as checking on a neighbor, sharing a skill, making someone laugh or finding a way to contribute to a community you care about.

All—yes, all—of the people I spoke with found meaning in service, volunteering and showing up for others. Their stories were a reminder that purpose doesn’t have to be grand or glamorous. Sometimes it’s simply knowing that someone else’s day was a little better because you were part of it.

Keep making room for things that make you feel alive

Play isn’t just for kids! Whether it’s dancing, learning a skill, exploring a new place or doing something that makes you laugh until you can’t catch your breath, enjoyment deserves a place in your life—even when you have a thousand other things to do.

You can also make a habit of noticing the good things that are already there. One simple way to do this is to keep a daily gratitude journal. Another idea? Take a picture of things that make you happy when you see them, then put them into a digital scrapbook that you can keep adding to.

The goal isn’t to turn happiness into another assignment on your to-do list; it’s to give you more opportunities to find happiness organically.

If you do this, how long will it be before you feel the change?

“The nice thing about happiness is that even small changes can lead to an immediate happiness boost,” Dr. Waldinger says. Help someone today, even just give someone new a compliment, and see how you feel. However, to feel a change in your general baseline mood, it might take a bit longer. Expect a couple of months for the habits to feel automatic. After a year, you’ll see some real gains in well-being.

And don’t feel defeated if you fall off the bandwagon. It happens to the best of us! Accept the slip as a normal part of being human, not as a referendum on your own worth, Dr. Waldinger says. In fact, the UC Berkeley study found that judging your own happiness only adds negative feelings. So cut the “I should be feeling happy …” and replace it with “I’m feeling upset right now, and that’s normal and OK—here’s what I am going to do differently tomorrow.” You can and will recover from a bad day, a bad month or even a bad year.

Is it too late to start?

Of course not! You’ll have days when you don’t feel happy, weeks when your plans fall apart and stretches when finding the energy to do much of anything feels harder than usual. That’s being human, not failing at happiness. The point isn’t to be cheerful all the time. It’s to keep making room for connection, curiosity and things that give your life meaning—even when you’re having a rough patch.

And it’s never too late to start something new. Just ask Natalie Grabow, our 80-year-old Ironman champion.

“I didn’t even learn to swim until I was 59 years old!” she tells me. “People think motivation fades with age. But if anything, it gets clearer.”

Maybe that’s the real secret: You don’t have to figure out how to be happy forever. In fact, there’s no such thing as happiness forever. Instead, keep living, keep connecting with others, stay aware of what does make you happy and stay open to whatever tomorrow brings.

articles.title: Everyone Is Obsessed with Peptides Right Now—Should You Take the Plunge?
articles.content:
“It feels like no one really knows what we’re doing by taking peptides,” says Margo Fleming, a 41-year-old ultramarathon runner in Los Angeles. Fleming started using BPC-157, a synthetic peptide that allegedly boosts wound healing and supports recovery, two years ago after hearing recommendations from several health professionals, including a personal trainer, a massage therapist and a naturopath. “I’ve dealt with a lot of injuries in the past, but I feel like my body is more resilient on peptides,” she says. Fleming says some of her chronic injuries—Achilles tendinitis and frequent calf strains—are gone.
Peptides are the body’s messengers that signal your cells to execute functions like prompting your kidneys to absorb water or your brain to release oxytocin. They occur naturally in your body, but synthetic versions, like the ones Fleming uses, can also be made in a laboratory and injected or swallowed to induce a variety of vital functions at will. Once limited to die-hard fitness circles, injectable peptides have seeped into the mainstream thanks to a heavy push on social media and widespread use of GLP-1 medications, which themselves are weight-loss peptides.
And there’s a peptide for nearly everything—speeding muscle recovery, slowing aging, helping a variety of injuries and ailments—though many aren’t well studied or approved for use by the Food and Drug Administration. Still, they’ve been publicly supported by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who announced in February that he planned to ease restrictions on 14 peptides that the FDA had previously banned pharmacies from creating. However, even Kennedy admitted that there isn’t much scientific evidence to support the use of supplemental peptides.
Health-care providers are usually wary of patients trying these so-called “gray market” products manufactured without FDA oversight. Meanwhile, desperate consumers are tempted by a buffet of choices.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more trends, knowledge, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
The term peptides can be confusing. “Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the same building blocks that make up proteins, just much smaller,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, chair of the Department of Kinesiology at McMaster University in Ontario. Several medications fall into the peptides category, including insulin and GLP-1s like Ozempic. Those are FDA approved; the peptides many people reference on social media are not.
“Your body makes thousands of them naturally, and they act as signaling molecules that tell cells what to do, whether that’s releasing a hormone, building tissue, regulating appetite or modulating inflammation,” Phillips says. “The peptides people are talking about now are synthetic versions designed to mimic or amplify those natural signals.”
Of the injectable and oral peptides popular on social media, BPC-157 (tied to muscle and tendon repair and gut health), is one of the most common, along with MK-677 (muscle growth), and SS-31 and GHK-Cu (both anti-aging). Influencers make bold claims about these products, suggesting that they can support gut health, muscle recovery, longevity and more. (Often, these influencers offer a discount code for an online retailer or provide a special link in their profile, suggesting that they receive a commission from sales.)
Because many peptides are not FDA approved, people often purchase products labeled for research use only, says Daniel T. Abazia, PharmD, director of the Rutgers/RWJBarnabas Health Medication-Use Safety and Information Center. But purchasing products labeled “not for human consumption” or “for research purposes only” means bypassing key safety checks.
About four years ago, Jessi Smith, a 33-year-old in Boston, developed a mysterious array of symptoms, including brain fog, fatigue, dizziness and food intolerances. Her functional medicine provider determined that she had mold toxicity and spent two years trying to help her feel better.
“It was getting to the point where we had tried everything,” Smith says. “We’re still detoxing the mold, still healing my gut. My immune system is just shot.” It was then that Smith’s provider suggested she try peptides as a way to “jump-start” her health.
She started with a blend of several peptides: BPC-157, KPV, GHK-Cu and N-acetyl larazotide. At first, she didn’t like the way she felt. She had “horrible insomnia” and felt awful the next day. “I don’t want to necessarily blame the peptides, because my body is pretty reactive right now,” she says. Smith restarted the peptide blend at a lower dose a few weeks later and felt better. “I still need to give it some time and ease up to the full dose, but thankfully had no bad reactions other than some fatigue the first few days,” she says.
Fleming’s experience has been different. “I have had no side effects,” she says. She had “pretty intense” tendinitis in her Achilles tendon for three years that went away after she started taking BPC-157. “I was in a space of seeing a podiatrist, getting prescriptions for MRIs … it was bad,” she says. “I recover faster on peptides.” She has also struggled with digestive-health issues for years. “Apparently BPC-157 helps with gut-related issues,” she says, “but I can’t say that anything is worlds better there.”
While BPC-157 is popular in athletic circles, it’s banned in and out of competition by the World Anti-Doping Agency, making it something that athletes competing at the national or international level, especially top finishers and record breakers, should avoid. (Fleming says she’s not running races to try to win.)
There is rigorous data to support the use of FDA-approved peptides, but clinical data on the unregulated wellness and sports peptides sold online is limited or lacking. One 2018 study found that BPC-157 helped heal damaged tendon-muscle junctions in rats given the peptide. And an earlier study, from 1996, found that when a group of adults ages 64 to 81 took MK-677, their levels of an important growth hormone were restored to those of young adults. But the study was small, including only 32 adults.
“A lot of peptides being used on the gray market currently don’t have human studies or have very limited human studies that are not ideal,” says Tracy Verrico, DO, a board-certified OB-GYN and hormone expert at Bona Dea Gynecology. “We definitely need more data. That’s what I’m telling patients.”
There’s also a big difference between animal and human studies, notes Abazia. “A peptide that heals a tendon in a rat doesn’t always work the same way in a 51-year-old man with a complex medical history,” he says.
Phillips says the lack of data to support these peptides is particularly concerning. “We have very limited human data,” he explains. “A lot of the enthusiasm is built on rodent studies, in vitro work, or anecdotes. That doesn’t mean these compounds don’t work, but we don’t really know what they do over months or years of use, what the right dose is, who shouldn’t take them or what happens when you stack three or four together, which is common practice.”
Phillips stresses that a lack of data isn’t evidence that these peptides are harmful. “But it’s also not evidence of safety, and the marketing tends to blur that distinction,” he says.
There’s also a lack of data on how well oral peptides perform compared to the more popular injectable peptides. “A capsule from a wellness website is almost certainly not delivering what an injection would,” Phillips says, noting that peptides are “poorly absorbed” when they’re taken orally.
But injectable peptides carry risks of infection and injection-site reaction, and then there’s the question of what’s actually in the vial, Phillips says.
Fleming acknowledges the lack of data surrounding peptides. “I feel like if there was some sort of glaring issue, I would stop,” she says. “I don’t know if this is blind optimism, but if I feel good, that’s good.” Fleming says she thinks the impact of BPC-157 has been “significant” on her health and fitness recovery but adds, “I really wish I could prove the peptides were helping.”
Many people who use peptides started them after feeling as if they had exhausted their options with conventional medicine. “I was getting no answers. I was told it was just anxiety,” Smith says. “I feel like I was getting very gaslit. The nontraditional routes have been more helpful for me.”
Peptides are often marketed to these patients. “A lot of people—particularly those dealing with chronic pain, slow recovery from injury, midlife metabolic changes or symptoms that don’t fit neatly into a diagnostic box—feel unheard by conventional medicine,” Phillips says. “Peptides are being marketed as a personalized, optimization-focused alternative, often by clinicians who spend more time listening than a typical primary-care visit allows.”
There can be a placebo effect to feeling cared for, he adds, noting that this “shouldn’t be dismissed.” Couple that with many social media claims, and it’s easy to see why some people are willing to try peptides. But before turning to them, take a step back. “Be honest with yourself about what you’re trying to fix,” Phillips says. “Many of the things that people use peptides for—recovery, body composition, energy—are far more responsive to consistent training, adequate protein and good sleep.”
If your current health-care provider isn’t meeting your care needs, Dr. Verrico suggests finding a new one. “If you feel that you’re not getting anywhere and you’re not being heard, you need to get a new doctor who will take the time to put the pieces together,” she says. “It may be someone who is offering [both] conventional and functional medicine.”
Dr. Verrico acknowledges the allure of peptides as a cure-all, though. “Peptides are pitched as the next best thing to sliced bread,” she says. “I know you’re desperate to feel better. Let’s figure [it] out in a safe way.”

articles.title: To Whom “Whom” May Concern: How Ellen Jovin Got People Across America Talking About Grammar
articles.content:
Suffering from punctuation paralysis? Semicolon confusion? End-of-sentence prepositions rage? Relax! The grammar guru, aka Ellen Jovin, will see you now. Or maybe she saw you already. Jovin has set up her Grammar Table in all 50 states, taking on every question posed by passersby, from the basic they’re vs. their to the eternally vexing lay vs. lie. And what she’s learned in her travels is this: Grammar is everywhere. We can’t escape it, even though many of us try. But love it, as Jovin does?
“I think it’s completely thrilling to be able to look at a sentence and know how many clauses and prepositional phrases there are, whether the verbs are transitive or intransitive, what the pronoun case is and so on,” she says. “I would have been ecstatic if we had spent additional years on grammar in school.”
In September 2018, Jovin, then an author, lecturer and communications coach for Syntaxis—her business that focuses on teaching communication workshops to businesses—was spending days cooped inside her apartment working on her language-learning blog as well as interacting in dozens of Facebook language groups. As the walls slowly began to close in on her, she had a revelation: I gotta get out of here!
“I didn’t want to spend that many hours a day online,” she says. Instead, “I wanted to use language in the real world for actual communication.”
So she stepped out of her apartment and set up a folding table across the street. Jovin, decked out in a leopard-print jacket, goofy ball-shaped earrings and a “Grammar Hedonist” T-shirt, was ready to laugh with everyone. She drew them little punctuation charts. She let them vent. As she told passersby: “I am here to answer grammar questions or take complaints.”
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more heartwarming stories, grammar tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
That December, she and her husband, Brandt Johnson, decided to take the show on the road, with Johnson filming what would become a documentary called Rebel with a Clause. True, he had never made a movie before. He’d done a lot of other things—acting, writing, even playing pro basketball in Europe touring against the Harlem Globetrotters. But mostly he and Jovin together run Syntaxis. That means they have the same boss—themselves—and could take off as soon as they wanted. So they did.
Those the couple met in their travels from Martha’s Vineyard to Flattop Mountain, Alaska, included kids, cops, lawyers, tourists, prom-goers, some grammar snob know-it-alls who got it all wrong, and two charming but inebriated young men with a pressing question. In Jovin’s book, also titled Rebel with a Clause, we meet Jason and Jack in Decatur, Alabama, after they’ve ambled over to her table to ask where the apostrophe goes in y’all. Jason wondered if it went before or after the a. Jack thought it didn’t go anywhere and y’all was just yall. Jovin explained that there is indeed an apostrophe and that it goes between the y and the all, because it’s taking the place of the rest of the word you.
The guys weren’t finished. While he and Jack helped themselves to her lunch, Jason asked what you call the “dot dot dot” you see when some words are missing.
“This is called an ellipsis,” said Jovin.
“I thought an ellipsis was the little …” Jason drew an oval in the air.
That’s an ellipse in math, Jovin explained. But in grammar it means something else and can be fun to talk about at parties. The plural is ellipses.
“I don’t normally talk to girls that are smart enough to know what that is,” Jason replied. “I need to find some girls that know what an ellipses is.”
He corrected himself: “What ellipses are.”
One sunny spring day in New York City, I accompanied Jovin to Central Park, where she set up her table and was soon swamped with queries.
“I still never get who and whom right,” said Linda Klein, a tourist from Los Angeles who was visiting with her dad, George Klein. “Do you have a trick for remembering it?”
Jovin smiled. She lives for such exchanges. While it all depends on context, she told Linda, there is a way to figure it out. Who is pretty much the equivalent of he, she and I—a subject. Whom is pretty much the equivalent of him, her or me—an object. And the way to figure which to use, Jovin continued, is to rephrase the sentence it’s in.
To use an example from Jovin’s book: If you’re trying to figure out what goes in the sentence “Evan, who/whom I thought was an honest person, plagiarized two paragraphs of mine,” you slice away everything outside of the commas. Then you consider whether you’d say “I thought he was an honest person” or “I thought him was an honest person.” Since it’s he, you use who.
But when it’s “Evan, who/whom I admired, just robbed a bank,” you take away what’s outside the commas and realize that Jovin admired him, not he. So you discover it’s whom, not who. Also that Evan is someone Jovin should steer clear of. (Yes—we’ll get to this point in a minute. It’s perfectly fine to end a sentence with a preposition, including of.)
Jovin and the Kleins continued to chat. Grammar is often an icebreaker, just as Jovin hoped. It turns out that George grew up in Czechoslovakia but also speaks Spanish (as does Jovin) and German (as does Jovin) and Hungarian, French and Russian (she’s got the French and a little Russian). Jovin has studied 28 languages and is currently brushing up on her Italian and Portuguese. She apologized to George for not having a Czech dictionary with her that day, though she did have a Polish one. Jovin always brings along a foreign language dictionary or two to help out in case people who speak those languages come to chat.
Linda had one last question: What does Jovin call herself? A therapist? “A roving grammarian,” Jovin answered.
As the Kleins were about to leave, another man strolled up. His name? Bill Funt. Was he possibly related to Alan Funt, creator of Candid Camera? Yup. That was his dad. This Funt was not fishing for the kind of squirmy moments that made his dad famous, but he did pose a couple of tough questions. First, he wondered if there was a nongendered word for aunt or uncle. After all, he said, the nongendered word for niece or nephew is nibling (a term coined by linguist Samuel E. Martin in the 1950s).
Jovin said she didn’t know of such a word, at least not in English.
“OK,” Funt continued. “My father, before he married my mom, was married and had three children. Then they divorced. Is there a word for what she [the first wife] is to me?”
“I have this same situation in my family,” Jovin replied. But there is, in fact, no special word, she said.

The holidays are coming, which means family gatherings and at least one relative telling a story you’ve heard a hundred times. (You know the one.) But between the food and festivities, there’s an opportunity most of us overlook: learning more about our family history. After all, when else do you have so many people who know so much about your past gathered in one place? And we’re not just talking about digging up old family secrets (though those can be pretty juicy). Your relatives are living connections to people, places and stories you may never get another chance to hear about. The trick is knowing what family history questions to ask.
To help you get those conversations started, we tapped two experts from American Ancestors: David Allen Lambert, the company’s chief genealogist, and Sarah Quiat, the interim director for the Wyner Family Jewish Heritage Center. They shared the questions worth asking your relatives while you have the chance, whether you’re hoping to uncover surprising family stories or simply learn a little more about where you came from.
“Talking with relatives, especially those we see infrequently, allows them to reflect on their own lives and the lives of your shared ancestors before them,” Quiat says. “By passing what you learn from them to the next generation of your family, or to genealogical researchers, you create invaluable and unique sources of information that might not be found anywhere else.”
Read on for the questions to ask your relatives this holiday season, along with how to record them for future generations. You might be surprised by what you learn about your family—and yourself.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holiday tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
The best way to start is to keep things casual. You don’t need to turn Thanksgiving dinner into a formal family interview to uncover great stories. Sometimes, a simple question like “How did you celebrate this holiday growing up?” is enough to get everyone talking. From there, you can ask about the relatives, traditions and memories that come up naturally.
If you want to preserve those stories, though, Quiat recommends hitting record. “Video recording is ideal, because you can see and hear someone telling their stories,” she says. And you don’t need fancy equipment. A smartphone works just fine, as long as your relative is comfortable being recorded.
For a more structured approach, set aside time for a one-on-one conversation, prepare a few questions and find somewhere quiet where you won’t be interrupted. Quiat also recommends getting permission on camera, as well as beginning with your names, the date, the location and what you’ll be discussing. You can bring out old photographs or family keepsakes to help spark memories too. And don’t feel you have to capture everything in one sitting. Consider your relative’s energy level, and remember that different family members may recall the same event differently, so it’s worth talking to several people.
Most importantly, don’t let the pressure to do it perfectly stop you from starting. As Quiat notes, “getting something is better than waiting to get it perfect and never getting the chance.”
The best way to uncover your family’s history is to ask the people who lived it, and the right questions can reveal surprising details you never knew about your relatives. According to Lambert and Quiat, here’s what to ask:
According to Quiat, one of the most important questions people forget to ask their relatives is: What advice would you give to future generations? “It can be of great value and insight to what was most important to the family member being interviewed, and it also actively brings the person listening into the picture,” she explains. It’s a chance to discover what your loved ones value most, what lessons they’ve learned and what wisdom they hope to pass down. Who knows? Their words might be exactly what a future grandchild needs to hear someday.
And don’t forget to dig into the little details behind your family’s biggest milestones. “Genealogists yearn for details, and an interview may reveal details about an event which you may only know names and dates,” says Lambert. For example, you might know when your grandparents got married, but do you know how they first met? Who made the first move? Lambert recommends asking relatives how they met their spouses or even how their own parents and grandparents fell in love. These conversations can uncover “a deep emotional memory that is never included in genealogical records and is often lost to time,” he says. After all, the dates might be written down somewhere, but it’s the stories behind them that really bring your family history to life.
Quiat and Lambert recommend capturing the kind of information you can’t easily find in records. Think old photographs, letters, diaries and family keepsakes, including who has them and where they’re stored. These little pieces of the past can tell you just as much about your family as the names and dates on a family tree.
There are also more personal parts of family history worth exploring, though they may call for a different conversation. Medical history, for example, can reveal important information about conditions that run in the family, but it’s not necessarily something to bring up during a casual interview about childhood memories. The same goes for sensitive subjects like adoption, divorce or painful family experiences.
“Proceed with caution, and ask the person you’re interviewing what they’re comfortable sharing,” says Quiat. It also matters what you plan to do with their answers. Someone might be happy to share a personal story privately but feel differently about having it recorded or shared with the wider family. The key is to make room for those conversations without making anyone feel pressured to share more than they want to.
You’ve asked the questions, heard the stories and maybe even uncovered a few family secrets. Now comes the important part: making sure those memories don’t get lost. Before you do anything else, back up your recordings, notes and photos. “It’s devastating to have a long conversation and lose it if your phone or recording device is damaged,” Quiat says. Her advice? “Ensure it lives in more than one place and has a digital backup.”
Once everything is safely saved, organize your findings in a way that’s easy to revisit. You might create digital folders for different relatives, put together a family history scrapbook or compile recordings and photographs into a collection everyone can access. And don’t keep all those fascinating discoveries to yourself! “Your family stories will only live on if you pass them down,” Quiat says. She recommends sharing your materials with relatives, friends or whoever will be responsible for preserving them in the future.
Want to make sure those stories survive for generations? Consider donating your materials to an archive. “An archive is the safest place for your family stories to ensure they will stay organized, preserved and waiting for future generations to explore,” Quiat says. You can contact local oral-history projects or archives to see if they’ll accept your collection. After all, the stories you save today could become the family treasures someone discovers decades from now.

  • What did your parents and grandparents do for a living?
  • What are some of your favorite memories of relatives who have since passed away?
  • What important lessons did your parents, grandparents or other elders teach you?
  • Are there any surprising, unusual or little-known stories about relatives who are no longer alive?

Questions about family history and ancestry

  • Do you know when and why our family first immigrated to this country?
  • Where did your parents, grandparents or earlier ancestors live before you were born?
  • Has our family surname ever changed, been shortened or been spelled differently? If so, what’s the story behind it?
  • Did anyone in our family serve in the military? Which branch did they serve in, where were they stationed and what do you know about their experiences?
  • Are there any old family photographs, letters, certificates or documents that could help us learn more about our ancestors?

Questions about family traditions and celebrations

  • How did your family celebrate holidays and birthdays when you were growing up?
  • What family traditions did your parents or grandparents pass down to you?
  • Are there any family traditions you wish we still practiced today?

Questions about school and education

  • What schools did you attend, and what do you remember most about them?
  • Was there a teacher or mentor who had a particularly big influence on your life?
  • Did you participate in any school clubs, sports or extracurricular activities?
  • Did you attend college or pursue any other education or training after finishing school?
  • Do you still have any school photographs, yearbooks, diplomas or other keepsakes?

Questions about their teenage years and social life

  • How did you and your friends spend your free time as teenagers?
  • What clubs, community groups or organizations were you involved in when you were younger?
  • Who were the most important friends in your life during your teenage years and early adulthood?
  • How did your social life and friendships change as you got older?

Questions about their first jobs and careers

  • What was your first job, where did you work and what do you remember about the experience?
  • What other jobs or careers have you had throughout your life?
  • Were there any employers, co-workers or professional mentors who had a lasting impact on you?

Questions about love, marriage and raising a family

  • How did you meet the person you ended up marrying?
  • What do you remember about your engagement or the moment you decided to get married?
  • What was your wedding day like, and where did you go on your honeymoon?
  • What do you remember most about the days your children were born?
  • What are some of your favorite memories of raising your children?

Questions about major historical events

  • What major historical events have had the biggest impact on your life?
  • How did those events affect your family, neighborhood or community?
  • Were you ever personally involved in a major historical event, social movement or period of change? What was your experience like?
  • Where were you when you first heard about a major news event you’ll never forget, and how did you react?

Questions about loss, remembrance and family health history

  • What do you remember about the final years or days of relatives who have passed away?
  • Are there any illnesses or health conditions that have affected multiple generations of our family?
  • How did your family traditionally honor loved ones who passed away, including funeral or burial customs?
  • What stories or memories would you most want future generations to know about relatives who are no longer with us?

  • When you were young, what did you want to do for a living, and did you end up pursuing that career?
  • Did your parents want you to have a career path that you didn’t pursue?
  • Did you ever want to live in a specific place—a city or country?
  • Did you think about getting married and/or having children when you were young? What kind of romantic partner did you dream about meeting?

  • Did your parents take you on vacations when you were a child?
  • Describe a trip you took as a child and what you remember about it.
  • Do still have a bucket list of places you want to visit? Why those places?
  • Did your parents play sports, and did you ever attend major sporting events?
  • Describe the first trip you took on your own (without your parents) and what that was like for you.
  • What’s the farthest place from home you’ve ever visited?
  • What’s the most beautiful place you’ve ever seen?
  • What would you consider your biggest travel adventure?

Questions about their biggest accomplishments and proudest moments

  • What were you good at as a child?
  • Did you ever win an award for something you did?
  • Do you have a story about your parents or immediate family that stands out as a proud moment?
  • Did a teacher or parent ever tell you they were proud of you for something?
  • What are you most proud of achieving in your life?

Questions about what makes them happy

  • What made you happy when you were a child?
  • Do you have a hobby or activity you do regularly that brings you joy?
  • Name three things that make you truly happy.
  • Describe some of the happiest times you’ve experienced in your life.
  • What do you think people should do if they want to be happier?

Questions about life lessons and advice

  • When you were young, did your parents or another adult give you any specific advice you remember?
  • Was that advice good, and does it still resonate with you today?
  • What advice would you offer from your own experiences to others?
  • What obstacles in life did you overcome?
  • What do you want future generations to remember most about you?
  • Has a friend or relative ever shared an important life lesson with you?
  • What has life taught you?

What’s the one question people usually forget to ask and then regret?

According to Quiat, one of the most important questions people forget to ask their relatives is: What advice would you give to future generations? “It can be of great value and insight to what was most important to the family member being interviewed, and it also actively brings the person listening into the picture,” she explains. It’s a chance to discover what your loved ones value most, what lessons they’ve learned and what wisdom they hope to pass down. Who knows? Their words might be exactly what a future grandchild needs to hear someday.

And don’t forget to dig into the little details behind your family’s biggest milestones. “Genealogists yearn for details, and an interview may reveal details about an event which you may only know names and dates,” says Lambert. For example, you might know when your grandparents got married, but do you know how they first met? Who made the first move? Lambert recommends asking relatives how they met their spouses or even how their own parents and grandparents fell in love. These conversations can uncover “a deep emotional memory that is never included in genealogical records and is often lost to time,” he says. After all, the dates might be written down somewhere, but it’s the stories behind them that really bring your family history to life.

What else is important to know about your family history?

Quiat and Lambert recommend capturing the kind of information you can’t easily find in records. Think old photographs, letters, diaries and family keepsakes, including who has them and where they’re stored. These little pieces of the past can tell you just as much about your family as the names and dates on a family tree.

There are also more personal parts of family history worth exploring, though they may call for a different conversation. Medical history, for example, can reveal important information about conditions that run in the family, but it’s not necessarily something to bring up during a casual interview about childhood memories. The same goes for sensitive subjects like adoption, divorce or painful family experiences.

“Proceed with caution, and ask the person you’re interviewing what they’re comfortable sharing,” says Quiat. It also matters what you plan to do with their answers. Someone might be happy to share a personal story privately but feel differently about having it recorded or shared with the wider family. The key is to make room for those conversations without making anyone feel pressured to share more than they want to.

What should you do with this information?

You’ve asked the questions, heard the stories and maybe even uncovered a few family secrets. Now comes the important part: making sure those memories don’t get lost. Before you do anything else, back up your recordings, notes and photos. “It’s devastating to have a long conversation and lose it if your phone or recording device is damaged,” Quiat says. Her advice? “Ensure it lives in more than one place and has a digital backup.”

Once everything is safely saved, organize your findings in a way that’s easy to revisit. You might create digital folders for different relatives, put together a family history scrapbook or compile recordings and photographs into a collection everyone can access. And don’t keep all those fascinating discoveries to yourself! “Your family stories will only live on if you pass them down,” Quiat says. She recommends sharing your materials with relatives, friends or whoever will be responsible for preserving them in the future.

Want to make sure those stories survive for generations? Consider donating your materials to an archive. “An archive is the safest place for your family stories to ensure they will stay organized, preserved and waiting for future generations to explore,” Quiat says. You can contact local oral-history projects or archives to see if they’ll accept your collection. After all, the stories you save today could become the family treasures someone discovers decades from now.

About the experts

  • David Allen Lambert is the chief genealogist at American Ancestors. He is the author of 11 books, including A Guide to Massachusetts Cemeteries, and also serves as the tribal genealogist for the Massachusett Tribe at Punkapoag in Massachusetts. 
  • Sarah Quiat is the interim director of the Wyner Family Jewish Heritage Center, formerly known as the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), at American Ancestors. She is an alumna of Vassar College and is a trained oral historian.

articles.title: Is the Royal Family Cursed? Apparently One of Its Titles Is—Here’s the Spooky Story Behind the Superstition
articles.content:
Who would say no to a fancy royal title? I don’t know about you, but Your Royal Highness or even milady sound pretty great to me. Well, as it turns out, some titles are more of a curse than a blessing. In fact, there’s one title in the British royal family’s lineage that may literally be cursed!
We’re not just talking a little unlucky in love. We’re talking so bad that it’s effectively been banned from use. Yikes! Also, we’re totally intrigued, and we’re betting you are too.
So which title comes with a whole lot of baggage, and what happened to the royals to whom it was given? And could it ever be brought back from (ahem) the dead? We asked royal historian Tracy Borman, author of The Private Lives of the Tudors: Uncovering the Secrets of Britain’s Greatest Dynasty, to shed some light on the title no modern royal would likely ever want.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royals, history, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The Duke of Clarence. It’s a “rare title,” Borman explains, and notable because of the way its three doomed holders died. “Each of them met a fairly sudden and unfortunate death,” she explains. We’ll get to that in a minute, but first, a little history about how this title came to be.
This duchy was created by King Edward III in 1362 for his third son, Lionel of Antwerp. But while it seems safe to say that the monarch had good intentions, it brought Lionel everything but luck, and the “curse” started with him, its very first holder. Lionel was in his early 20s when he received the title. And given his age, he still had his life ahead of him—or at least that’s what he and his family thought. But nobody could have imagined what happened soon after.
They all died way before their time—and in very unusual circumstances. Coincidence or curse? Keep reading, and decide for yourself.
King Edward III’s third son was born in Antwerp (hence, the name) and married Violante Visconti, daughter of Galeazzo II Visconti, the Lord of Milan. Six years after becoming the Duke of Clarence—and only a couple of months into his second marriage, to Violante—he passed away.
“He was just shy of his 30th birthday,” Borman says. “And he died so suddenly that it was believed he’d been poisoned by his father-in-law.” Let’s just say the Visconti family had a reputation for ruthlessness and the whole “ends justify the means” mentality. Still, there’s no actual confirmation that Lionel’s death was the result of foul play.
Next came Thomas of Lancaster, second son of King Henry IV. He received the duchy when he was 24 or 25, in 1412. But this pairing was not meant to be. Borman notes that he was “very active on the battlefield and in government,” and he died while defending his country—but not particularly well. “He led the English in one of their most disastrous defeats to the French at the Battle of Baugé,” she says. “It was a fairly ill-advised attack, and he was killed at the age of 33.”
The most famous Duke of Clarence was George Plantagenet—brother of King Edward IV and King Richard III—who died a rather spectacular death at age 28. “He was the classic middle son of the three brothers, a kind of traitorous character who was not at all trusted by either of his siblings,” says Borman.
George tried to dethrone his brother Edward IV, who then had him convicted for treason. “Famously, it’s said that the Duke of Clarence was able to choose the manner of his death, so he decided to be drowned in Malmsey wine, which was, apparently, his favorite wine,” Borman says. While there’s no proof that this actually happened, “he’s definitely gone down in history for that.”
Technically, yes, but neither of them held the exact title Duke of Clarence—the two that got away both had extended versions of it. Plus, their lives weren’t all that rosy, as you’ll see.
Prince William Henry (1765–1837), also known as Duke of Clarence and St. Andrews, and later as King William IV, died of old age at 71. However, tragedy (and royal scandals) struck his home decades earlier: A notorious womanizer, William Henry had no less than 10 secret children with his mistress Dorothea Jordan, but he was pushed into marrying a more suitable woman, Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. The royal couple had two daughters together, but they both died in infancy.
The other one who escaped a mysterious death was Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale (1864–1892). He died young, at the age of 28, but he was simply a victim of an influenza pandemic. That being said, rumor has it that he carried a dark secret. “Some authors have theorized that he was London’s serial killer Jack the Ripper,” Borman says. Wait, what?! The famous killer, of course, terrorized East London in the late 1800s. He murdered at least five women, all of them prostitutes, and was never caught. Jack the Ripper’s identity is still a mystery today.
No. “It died out, as sometimes happens with ill-fated titles,” says Borman. While there’s no official explanation for this—and monarchs have generally been free to choose whatever title they wanted for their kids—Borman thinks the reason is likely because “there were three fairly bad ends met by Dukes of Clarence, [and] it’s therefore a title people didn’t really want.”
This doesn’t mean that the royals are particularly superstitious, although she adds, “historically, they probably were a bit.” Let’s be honest: Even if you don’t believe in curses, would you really take the risk and give that title to a loved one? The number of untimely deaths aside, there could be another reason why monarchs have shied away from the title. “The last real Duke of Clarence, George, was so notorious and such an enemy to the Crown that the idea of creating another Duke of Clarence was pretty abhorrent,” Borman says. Fair point!
Yes, but considering what happened to the previous holders, it seems highly unlikely. Rumor had it for a while that Kate and William’s youngest son, Prince Louis, could be named the next Duke of Clarence once William becomes king. But this probably won’t happen. “Historically speaking, you’ve got to be careful with titles,” Borman says. “If there’s any negative association, then people can be quite cautious about bringing them back.”
Plus, we just can’t imagine that Kate or William would want their son associated with a late duke who got drowned in liters of wine and another who tried to overthrow the reigning monarch—and his own brother!
